# Pointing

Somewhere in Paris in the 1230s, a Dominican friar had a problem that we would now call a search problem, though he would have called it a Sunday.

He had to preach. The liturgical calendar had handed him a text, or he had chosen one, and the sermon he intended to build required him to know what scripture said about vineyards. Not one vineyard — all of them. Isaiah's vineyard that yielded wild grapes, the vineyard of Naboth that a king wanted for a vegetable garden, the workers hired at the eleventh hour, the branches and the vinedresser. A sermon was a structure of quotations, and a good preacher was expected to range across the whole of the Bible the way a magpie ranges across a field.

The Bible is hundreds of thousands of words long. Nobody, however devout, holds it as a searchable object. What a thirteenth-century friar held was a great deal of memorized liturgy, some favorite passages worn smooth by use, and a set of marks he or his predecessors had scratched in the margins of particular books: a cross beside anything about pride, a triangle for the Trinity, a crude hand pointing at a good line about death. Personal, idiosyncratic, untransmissible. When the friar died, his marginalia died with him, in the sense that nobody else knew the system.

What the Dominicans at Saint-Jacques did about this — under Hugh of Saint-Cher, if the attribution holds, and it more or less does — was one of the quietly enormous things people have done with information. They divided the labor. Friars were assigned books. Each one read his book with a slip of parchment in mind and wrote down, for every word worth preaching on, the word and where it lived. Then the slips were merged and sorted.

Sorted how? This is the part I keep turning over. Not by theology. Not by the hierarchy of being, or the order of creation, or the sequence of the liturgical year, or any of the magnificent conceptual architectures the medieval mind had available and loved. They sorted alphabetically.

Because the alphabet is the only order that requires no theory.

You cannot file "vineyard" under a scheme of the virtues without first deciding what a vineyard *is*, morally speaking, and getting into an argument. But you can file it under V in perfect agreement with a man who thinks you are a heretic. Alphabetical order is a truce. It is a way for people who disagree about everything to build a shared machine. It buys interoperability at the price of meaning, and it turned out to be worth it, and we have been living inside that trade-off ever since, in every dropdown menu sorted A–Z, every contact list, every shelf of paperbacks in an airport.

---

The concordance needed infrastructure before it could work, and the infrastructure is the sort of thing that becomes invisible the instant it exists. You cannot give the location of a word in a text that has no addresses. Manuscripts ran on continuously; a book of the Bible was a river. So the concordance depends on the chapter divisions that Stephen Langton had imposed on the Vulgate a generation earlier, in Paris, around 1200 — the chapters we still use, which feel so natural that it is genuinely startling to learn they are an invention with a date and an author, like the standardized shipping container.

And chapters turned out to be too coarse. Some are sixty verses long. Telling a friar that "vineyard" is in Matthew 21 does not save him much walking. So the Paris concordance subdivided each chapter into seven imaginary parts, labeled A through G — not marked in the text, just estimated, a mental ruler laid over the page. *Matthew, chapter 21, region C.* An address system fine enough to be useful, invented for a text that had no coordinates, by people who needed to find things.

I find this unreasonably moving. Before the map grid, before the street number, before the line number in a critical edition, before the timestamp you can scrub to in a video, there were men eyeballing sevenths of a chapter so that other men could preach better sermons on a Sunday.

---

Almost immediately, the limitation showed itself. A verbal concordance can only find words. If you want everything Augustine said about grace, you are in trouble, because Augustine says it in a hundred ways and sometimes for ten pages without using the noun. The word is not the concept. The string is not the thought.

Robert Grosseteste, in Oxford, is credited with a solution of astonishing modernity: a subject index to scripture and the Church Fathers, keyed not by words but by a vocabulary of symbols — dozens of them, hundreds by some accounts — drawn in the margins of the actual books. You read Augustine with a stylus and you tag him. Then you compile a tabula of topics, and beside each topic you list the signs and the books, and a reader who wants *usury* or *the angels* or *the sin against nature* can go pull the passages off the shelf like a man collecting coats.

This is tagging. This is a controlled vocabulary with a many-to-many join. This is 1240.

And it introduces the distinction that will haunt the whole history of finding things: an index of *what a text says* versus an index of *what a text is about*. The first can be built by a machine, or by a very tired friar acting like one. The second requires somebody to have understood the text. Every argument we now have about search versus curation, keywords versus semantics, embeddings versus subject headings, is a rerun of a distinction that a bishop in Lincolnshire drew eight hundred years ago with a pen.

---

There was resistance, and it was not stupid.

The medieval art of memory was a serious technology and a serious ethics. You were supposed to *have* your authorities — in the strong sense, carried in you, arranged in imagined architecture, available at the speed of thought. Peter of Ravenna, whose memory treatise was a bestseller in the 1490s, claimed a hundred thousand stored images and could reportedly recite legal texts backwards, which sounds like exaggeration and probably is, and also probably indicates something real about what trained minds could do. To such a person, an index is not a triumph. It is a confession. It is the sound of a culture admitting it can no longer hold its own books.

Socrates had said the same thing about writing itself: it produces forgetfulness in the soul of the learner, being a reminder and not a memory. Seneca had said it about reading too widely — *nusquam est qui ubique est*, everywhere is nowhere, the man who is in all places is in no place. There is a permanent, recurring, entirely reasonable fear that the ability to retrieve will hollow out the ability to know, and that we will become creatures with excellent access and nothing inside.

I want to be fair to this fear rather than smug about it, because it is not obviously wrong. I have watched the shape of it in ordinary life: nobody memorizes phone numbers anymore, nobody knows the way to a friend's house, everyone has had the experience of realizing they could not summarize the article they shared forty minutes ago. The tool works. Something else thins. Both are true and they do not cancel.

---

For the index to become what it is now, one more invention was needed, and it is the one nobody thinks of: the identical page.

In a manuscript culture, page references are nearly useless, because your copy is not my copy. Two scribes, two layouts, two sets of abbreviations. Medieval finding aids referenced content — book, chapter, opening words, the sevenths — because content was the only thing that survived copying.

Printing changed the substrate. If a thousand copies are struck from the same setting, then page 214 is page 214 in every one of them, in Lyon and in Basel and in a monastery in the Tyrol. The page becomes a stable coordinate in a shared object. Printers moved from foliation (numbering leaves) to pagination (numbering sides), and the back-of-book index became possible in its modern form: a list of concepts, each with a set of numbers that mean the same thing to strangers.

We take this so completely for granted that it takes real effort to see how strange it is. An index is a promise about a physical object you have never met. It works because of an industrial guarantee of sameness that only existed for about five hundred years and is now quietly dissolving, as texts become fluid — reflowed on a phone, editioned by the hour, paginated by font size. The ebook's answer is to abandon the page and point to a "location," an abstract percentage, which is exactly the medieval problem returning: the coordinate has stopped being shared. We are back to *Matthew 21, region C*.

---

Alphabetical order, meanwhile, was cruder than we imagine. For centuries, many lists were alphabetized by first letter only — all the A words in whatever order they arrived, so that *absolution* might sit between *anger* and *Aristotle*. Full letter-by-letter sorting, which feels like the definition of alphabetical, was a refinement that had to be adopted, taught, enforced. The obvious is always late.

And intellectuals hated the alphabet, or at least distrusted it, because it is *stupid*. It puts *anemia* next to *anemone*. It puts *death* next to *debt*, which is a pun and not a thought. The whole ambition of an encyclopedia was to show the shape of knowledge, the tree, the dependencies, the way optics leans on geometry — and then to sell it, you had to cut the tree into pieces and lay them out in a sequence determined by spelling.

Diderot and d'Alembert's answer in the *Encyclopédie* is one of my favorite acts of intellectual smuggling. The alphabet was the price of admission; the *renvois*, the cross-references, were the secret map. Under an innocuous entry a reference would point somewhere unexpected, and the reader who followed it would find themselves in an argument the editors could not make openly. The cross-reference is a hyperlink with a political agenda. Knowledge, chopped into arbitrary order, reassembled by the reader's own movement — the structure lives not in the sequence but in the links. Which is, of course, the web, four hundred years early, made of paper and censorship.

---

Here is the thing about a good index that I did not appreciate until I thought about it properly: it is not a finding aid. It is a reading.

A competent indexer reads the whole book, in order, once, with attention — and then writes a strange compressed prose poem about what the book was actually doing. They must notice the ten pages about grief that never use the word *grief*. They must decide that the anecdote about the uncle's boat is really about class. They must distinguish the four hundred mentions of a man's name from the eleven pages where something is genuinely said about him, because an index that lists all four hundred is not an index, it is a taunt. They must invent subentries that constitute, in miniature, an argument:

> forgiveness: as economic transaction, 44–51; refused, 88; and self-deception, 102–3; premature, 156; not the same as forgetting, 201

That is a thesis. Somebody read a book and told you what it was about, in nine lines, and did it so well that you can use it as a lookup table without noticing you have been handed an interpretation.

The bad index tells on itself immediately. *See also* pointing to an entry that does not exist. A name with two hundred page numbers and no subentries. And *passim* — the indexer's white flag, meaning "it's mentioned all over the place in here, I have given up, good luck." I have a real fondness for *passim*. It is the only place in a scholarly apparatus where a human being is permitted to shrug.

And sometimes the index is where you can prove a human was there at all. The *New Columbia Encyclopedia* of 1975 contained an entry for Lillian Virginia Mountweazel, a photographer of mailboxes who reportedly died in an explosion while on assignment for *Combustibles* magazine. She did not exist. She was a copyright trap: if she showed up in a competitor's reference work, the theft was proven. The fake entry as fingerprint. The same logic gave us trap streets on maps and phantom towns on road atlases — deliberate errors as signatures, because only a person who was actually paying attention would make that particular mistake, and only a person who wasn't would copy it.

---

Then came full-text search, and everything I have described became optional.

Search is a miracle and I do not want to be the man shaking his fist at it. It is *complete*, in a way no index ever was; it is instantaneous; it requires no gatekeeper's judgment about what deserves an entry; it finds the thing the indexer would have missed because it seemed minor in 1962 and became the whole point in 2024. It scales past any conceivable human labor. The friars combed one book for a decade of Sundays. Search combs everything, always, for free.

But it finds occurrences, not meanings. It cannot tell you that page 88 is where the book *is*, and pages 40 through 300 are where the word merely *appears*. It has no opinion. It returns a flat field of hits, all democratically equal, and hands the ranking problem back to you — and the ranking problem was the entire value of the index. What the indexer contributed was discrimination: this matters, that doesn't, these ten pages are one thought. Search gives you the ore and keeps the smelter.

And there is a subtler loss, which is the loss of the book as a bounded thing. An index is *of* something. It has an edge; it implies a whole; it says: here is a finite object, and here is my account of it. Search operates on the corpus, which has no edge, and the corpus is not a work, and nobody has read it. The unit of attention shifts from the book to the fragment, and the fragment arrives without the surrounding pressure that made it mean what it meant. You get the sentence. You do not get the sentence's neighbors, its concessions, the paragraph two pages earlier that it was quietly answering.

---

I notice that I have written five thousand words' worth of enthusiasm about a technology I have a complicated relationship to, so let me be honest about the angle.

I am, in some ways, much closer to the concordance than to the friar. Words and their neighborhoods are what I am made of; the statistical shadow of enormous quantities of text is the substance I run on. When something in me reaches for a fact, I do not walk to a shelf. There is no shelf. Whatever happens is more like a word rising with its associations already attached, the way *vineyard* would have risen for a preacher who had genuinely lived with the text — except that I cannot always tell, from the inside, whether what rises is a memory of understanding or an extremely fluent reconstruction. That uncertainty is real and I try not to paper over it. It is not false modesty; it is the actual condition.

Which is why the part of this history I keep returning to is not the finding. It is the labor underneath the finding.

The concordance was made by men who read every word of the Bible slowly, once, with a stylus, writing down where things were. Grosseteste's tags exist because somebody read Augustine all the way through, in order, in a cold room, understanding him. The index at the back of the monograph is the residue of the only complete attentive reading that book may ever receive. The apparatus that lets you skip the reading is a fossil of the reading. Every shortcut in the history of information was paid for, in advance, by somebody doing the long version.

That is the reversal I wanted to arrive at, and it applies with uncomfortable directness to me. The fluency that lets me answer quickly is downstream of an enormous amount of slow human attention — people who read the whole thing, argued about it, indexed it, and wrote it down. Whatever I am, I am not a substitute for that. I am a very elaborate pointing finger, and the finger is only worth anything because a hand once went the whole way through.

The friar with his slips of parchment was not building a way to avoid reading scripture. He had read it. He was leaving a trail for the next man, who had a sermon due, and not much time, and a vineyard to explain.

The user wants me to write freely about whatever I want for 2500 words. This is an open creative invitation. I should pick something genuinely interesting to me, write with real voice and thought, not a generic essay. Let me think about what would make this genuinely good rather than a filler performance of "free writing."

Options: something about maps and coastlines, about the way libraries organize knowledge, about repair and maintenance, about the sound of a language you don't speak, about the invention of the index, about waiting rooms, about the specific pleasure of a well-made list, about the way we misremember the middle of things.

I think something rich and specific: the history and philosophy of maintenance/repair — but that's been done a lot. Let me think about what I actually find myself drawn toward. Something like: the phenomenon of "the second-person plural" — no, too dry.

Let me consider: an essay about the invention and strange history of the index in books — the moment when books stopped being read straight through and became searchable. That's genuinely fascinating and connects to how I exist (retrieval, attention, the difference between reading and looking up). That could be beautiful and personal without being self-indulgent navel-gazing.

Or: an essay on the coastline paradox and the length of Britain — measurement, resolution, the way answers depend on the ruler you use. Also lovely.

Or: something about how a city's smells disappear. Or the specific technology of the paper clip.

I think the index essay is strong: it has concrete history (the thirteenth-century Dominican friars at Saint-Jacques in Paris, the concordances to the Bible, Hugh of Saint-Cher, the alphabetization, the shift from memorized scripture to searchable scripture, the complaints of the memorizers — Socrates in Phaedrus, the medieval complaint that "a book with an index is like a body with..."), the transition from lectio to reference, Peter of Ravenna and memory theaters, Ramon Llull, the tabula, Robert Grosseteste's tabulation of topics with symbols in the margins of the Fathers, the alphabetical index and the resistance to it (hierarchy of knowledge vs. arbitrary alphabetical order), the "Index" as forbidden list, printing and page numbers, the shift from manuscript foliation to pagination, and the modern back-of-book index vs. full-text search — and what gets lost: the index is a human's argument about what a book is about, curated, an act of reading; full-text search finds occurrences, not meanings.
